The reuse is pretty bad, these are running daily so it just means 90% of mathlib is 'gone' after a day, typically. I think will increase the frequency here to 2 or 3 a day (I'm trying to keep under the free cloudflare limit of 10GB, but this should be fine)

Okay, I did end up asking Claude:

The new Lake cache leaves the underlying build artifacts (.olean etc.) ~95% byte-identical between the given commits, but because it transfers per-module .ltar bundles that embed each module's cascading input-hash trace, only ~550 modules are actually reused; essentially the same import-cone invalidation as the old cache.

So the content addressing doesn't do anything at this point :tired:

Ah! You beat me to it! :-)

Your message yesterday nudged me too and I was experimenting with lake to fix that. I can send more numbers / details later, but yeah changing this can save like 90% in storage in the long run
(and fetching for users! Let's not forget that part :) )
Yes! Exactly
I'm still polishing this a bit, but lean4#13992 is a proposal on how to store this metadata separately without extra roundtrips to the cache (cc @Mac Malone )

And some experiments (small N=18, arguably) gave me these projections:

Measured over 18 same-toolchain daily pairs across 3 toolchain windows (rc2 / v4.30.0 / rc1); compression 0.063 (bundle ≈51 KB/module); per-commit figures modeled from the depHash cascade (mean 97 MB/commit, ~950 commits/mo).

@Marcelo Lynch leantar already strips logs and the input tree.
The input hash is the relevant problem here. However, I am not sure if/how leantar makes use of that. We should ask @Mario Carneiro about that.
Ideally, leantar could support writing the input hash to the trace as part of unpacking.
Modulo leantar (I think the logs are not stripped btw...?), my PR also adds a local lookup path that skips fetching the ltars if the files already exist locally.
That should already be done in current Lake. That's what the other alternaitve of ModuleOutputs is for.
@Marcelo Lynch leantar does keep some logs (such as errors), but it strips the traces which contain platform-dependent CLI calls. This was considered important for debugging failed mathlib builds.

Mac Malone said:

That should already be done in current Lake. That's what the other alternaitve of ModuleOutputs is for.

I'm pretty sure I tested this empirically, I wonder what was missed. I think there might be no way to take that codepath without knowing the artifacts in advance, and the published mappings don't do that because data contains only the hash of the ltar itself?
If you already have the artifacts locally, you should not be going through the published mappings?
mm but what if you changed commits so there's new mappings and input hashes (coming from the remote that built this new commit), but the outputs are byte identical?
you shouldn't need to download anything, but you don't know that in advance

Currently, remote mappings take precedence over local ones (i.e., we rewrite all the cached inputs). This is intentional as Lake's trace can be underepresentative, and the principle of least suprise suggests that if you fetch a remote (cia an explicit cache get), you probably want that remote's artifacts (not potentially stale local artifacts). We could offer an option for cache get (e.g., --keep-local) that only overrides inputs if they do not yet exist.

we rewrite all the cached inputs

inputs in which sense?

Marcelo Lynch said:

mm but what if you changed commits so there's new mappings and input hashes (coming from the remote that built this new commit), but the outputs are byte identical?

here I meant that the new mapping from the remote (which has built the new commit that you just checked out to) is the source of truth, but data only has the ltar hash so you can't realy do the fastpath of checking if the (unpacked) outputs are already there on disk / the local CAS. I guess if ltar = f(outputs) then this is better and you will still skip the download, as long as the ltar is still around (but you still need to unpack it to figure out if the artifacts are already in place...)
It seems like carrying the actual output metadata in the mapping (given that it is bounded) is a good idea for stuff like this, it also lets you do stuff like rehashing to verify integrity, etc.

rehashing to verify integrity

bah, actually if the ltar is content addressed this makes no sense
Also, carrying the output metadata is multiplicative on the size of the mappings. Avoiding unnecessary data there can be quite beneficial.
(but here we're bypassing the ltar entirely in some cases)
well, honestly my first instinct was to store this in a separate file, but then I got more swayed about avoiding another roundtrip to the cache

Marcelo Lynch said:

we rewrite all the cached inputs

inputs in which sense?

The output (JSON data + some JSON metadata) of a single input is cached in the local Lake cache (as a JSON file named according to the input hash for a package).
I see. I think my scenario still stands, the authoritative mapping is the remote one there

Marcelo Lynch said:

here I meant that the new mapping from the remote (which has built the new commit that you just checked out to) is the source of truth, but data only has the ltar hash so you can't realy do the fastpath of checking if the (unpacked) outputs are already there on disk / the local CAS. I guess if ltar = f(outputs) then this is better and you will still skip the download, as long as the ltar is still around (but you still need to unpack it to figure out if the artifacts are already in place...)

If input-hash is the same then, then the remote cache is skipped entirely and the previous trace will be used (which will include the proper outputs). If the trace has changed, but the same content-addressed ltar was previously downloaded, then it will be in the local cache and no downloads are necessary. Assuming input overrides (the status quo), then an unpack will be needed, but that is already at least partially needed to update the trace in the build directory.
The experiment I had done was trying this with batteries and observing that in the maximal case (everything was local) there were 187 spawns of leantar (vs none) and 0.44s vs 0.13s
Did you remove the build directory? (Or was this changing commits?)
In general, I don't feel that runtime difference for restoring a build sufficiently justifies signficantly increasing the mappings size.

Mac Malone said:

Did you remove the build directory? (Or was this changing commits?)

I didn't remember, so I sent claude to rerun this experiment, it looks like it will do it even if everything is present

Claude says (oops)

With a fully up-to-date build directory, same commit, valid trace present, fetching the mapping (remote precedence) costs the baseline a complete re-unpack sweep on the very next build:

│ Intact build dir + fresh mapping fetch, same input hashes │ Time │ leantar spawns │
│ Baseline (current Lake) │ 0.54 s │ 187 │
│ Feature │ 0.13 s (= no-op) │ 0 │

The reason is code order, not staleness: in the artifact-cache-writable flow, fetchCore consults the outputs cache before the trace replay — and after a cache get the .ltar branch clears the build outputs and unpacks, never reaching the trace that would have said "up to date." The previous trace is not used; it's overwritten by the unpack. So under the status quo, every cache get in an existing workspace buys a full unpack sweep even when nothing changed at all.
Ah, I think I may have had a reason for the current order, but I forgot the details. It is certainly worth testing trying the trace before the local cache (a perhaps again afterwards).
I am hoping to do some work on the cache later this week (i.e., probably Friday), so I can take a look at some of this.
The big thing it sounds like we need, though, is to loop @Mario Carneiro into this and have leantar natively support depHash-less archives.
One advantage of having leantar emit the proper input hash is that can also ensure atomic correctness of the trace.
